projects.name: RAGenius
projects.headline: Answers that point back to the document.
projects.summary: Document Q&A for people who need to check the source. Retrieves PDF passages, attaches citations, and abstains when the evidence is missing.
results: 52/75 tasks passed in the committed evaluation
projects.resultNote: Developer-authored benchmark; not a production accuracy claim.
projects.problem: Finding an answer in a set of PDFs is only half the task. Readers also need to know which passage supports it, and when the system does not have enough evidence.
projects.approach: I split documents into overlapping chunks, embed them, and retrieve candidate passages with FAISS. A FastAPI service returns the answer and evidence, while a Streamlit interface makes the workflow accessible. The answering path includes citation and abstention checks.
projects.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[PDF documents] --> B[Chunks and embeddings]
  B --> C[FAISS retrieval]
  C --> D{Evidence available?}
  D -->|Yes| E[Answer with citations]
  D -->|No| F[Abstain]
projects.learning: The evaluation makes the tradeoff visible: citation coverage does not guarantee a useful answer. The committed report includes short-answer and keyword-miss failures, so improving answer completeness is a clearer next step than claiming the system is solved.
projects.limits: The report records 42/65 document-Q&A tasks passing and an average latency of 7.387 seconds for that run. Results depend on the document set, evaluation rules and hardware. A public hosted demo and genuine UI capture are still TODOs.

projects.name: Agent Orchestration
projects.headline: Specialists with a reviewer in the loop.
projects.summary: A task orchestration prototype that routes research and code work to specialists, reviews outputs, and records decisions in a structured trace.
results: Example trace records planning, dispatch, tools, review and synthesis
projects.resultNote: The README shows example runs; they are not a general performance benchmark.
projects.problem: A request can combine research and calculation. A single answer hides which tool ran, how the task was split, and whether a result was reviewed.
projects.approach: I use a LangGraph supervisor to plan and route subtasks, separate research and code specialists to execute them, and a reviewer to approve, retry or escalate. JSON traces capture the path from the original task to the final response.
projects.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[User task] --> B[Supervisor]
  B --> C[Research specialist]
  B --> D[Code specialist]
  C --> E[Reviewer]
  D --> E
  E -->|Approved| F[Synthesis]
  E -->|Rejected| G[Retry or human escalation]
projects.learning: A reviewer can be wrong when it judges new information using stale knowledge. The README documents a fix that supplies the current date and narrows rejection criteria to what the reviewer can actually assess. I would validate that change with a labeled benchmark before making an approval-rate claim.
projects.limits: The README contains a 15.51-second example trace, not a latency guarantee. Parallel execution, shared Redis state and cost tracking are roadmap items. A hosted demo, UI screenshot and measured routing benchmark are TODOs.

projects.name: RxSupply AI
projects.headline: AI proposes. Python checks. A person decides.
projects.summary: An evidence-grounded medicine supply prototype for operations teams. Validates model-selected facts against FDA records and prepares simulated replenishment plans for human review.
results: 10/10 small regression cases passed; LLM not evaluated by this suite
1,600 normalized records in the dated source snapshot
projects.resultNote: Developer-authored cases; procurement scenarios are synthetic.
projects.problem: Medicine supply review involves different evidence: national notices, local stock and a purchasing budget. A generated answer can blur those boundaries or invent facts that the source never contained.
projects.approach: I retrieve product records with SQLite FTS5 and BM25, ask an optional local model to select facts, and independently compare every proposed field/value against retrieved evidence. Missing or invalid evidence leads to abstention. A separate planning tool works with synthetic inventory under budget and supplier constraints.
projects.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Public FDA snapshot] --> B[SQLite BM25 retrieval]
  B --> C[Local LLM fact selection]
  C --> D[Python claim validator]
  D --> E[Evidence packet or abstention]
  F[Simulated inventory] --> G[Budget planning]
  E --> H[Human review]
  G --> H
projects.learning: Separating model proposals from deterministic validation makes failures inspectable. Exact source agreement is useful, but it cannot establish clinical suitability or local availability. The evaluation explicitly separates the extractive baseline from the optional LLM path.
projects.limits: This is a CLI and loopback-only JSON API prototype, not a deployed pharmacy service or clinical system. The 10-case regression suite does not evaluate LLM accuracy. A current screenshot and broader evaluation are TODOs.

projects.name: VerticalDesk
projects.headline: A proposed resolution before an incident is created.
projects.summary: An AI-assisted triage prototype for service teams: classifies a request, retrieves knowledge-base articles, drafts a cited resolution, and waits for human approval.
projects.resultNote: Repository-reported test count; not independently rerun for this portfolio.
projects.problem: A service request needs a category, priority, relevant knowledge and a destination. Automatically turning a draft into an incident would skip a useful review step.
projects.approach: I connect a React interface to a FastAPI backend and MongoDB. The pipeline classifies impact and urgency, retrieves knowledge-base context, drafts a resolution and proposes routing. A person approves or rejects the proposal before the write occurs; an ordered agent trace records the steps.
projects.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[Request] --> B[Classify]
  B --> C[Retrieve knowledge]
  C --> D[Draft and route]
  D --> E{Human approval}
  E -->|Approve| F[Create incident]
  E -->|Reject| G[Discard]
projects.learning: The boundary between a suggestion and a write matters. The project makes that boundary explicit with an approval gate, citations and a trace, rather than treating a plausible draft as a completed resolution.
projects.limits: The source repository is private. Its README image URLs are currently unavailable, so this page uses a labeled workflow illustration. Public demo, accessible screenshots and a measured triage-quality evaluation remain TODOs.

projects.name: JobLens MCP
projects.headline: Job context, one tool call away.
projects.summary: An MCP server for job seekers using AI assistants. Combines official job-search API results, local resume parsing and an explainable skill-overlap score.
results: Search, parse and match exposed as assistant tools
[TODO] Add a measured parsing and matching evaluation
projects.resultNote: Skill overlap is a transparent heuristic, not a hiring prediction.
projects.problem: An assistant needs current job listings and resume context to give useful search support. That context should not require storing a job-platform password or automating a logged-in browser.
projects.approach: I expose job search, local resume parsing and skill matching through FastMCP. An isolated Adzuna client supplies job listings while local parsing extracts resume fields. The match score reports matched and missing skills so the result can be inspected.
projects.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  A[AI assistant] --> B[FastMCP tools]
  B --> C[Adzuna API]
  B --> D[Local resume parser]
  C --> E[Skill overlap scoring]
  D --> E
  E --> F[Matched and missing skills]
projects.learning: Separating the job-data adapter from the tool layer keeps a provider change from spreading through the MCP interface. An explainable score is useful for search exploration, but should not be presented as an assessment of someone's ability.
projects.limits: An Adzuna API key and local MCP client are required. Hosted demo, genuine interface capture and measured parsing accuracy remain TODOs.
